lessons.title: What is your website?

explanation.text: Your browser displays the shop. The server answers requests. The database stores information. Think of a shop window, a shop assistant and a stock book: three different jobs.
The home page starts in app/page.tsx. Images and buttons are what you see. Product data can come from the server.

explanation.title: async / await
explanation.text: A function can wait for work to finish, such as loading products.

codeExample.code:
export default async function HomePage() {
  // Read the same live catalogue used by the app.
  const [dbProducts, heroImages, heroBanners, reviewStats, promotionProducts] = await Promise.all([
    getDbProducts({ activeOnly: true }),
    getHeroImages(),
    getHeroBanners(),
    getReviewStats(),

annotations.label: Next.js uses app/page.tsx to build the home page. HomePage prepares what visitors see; async lets it wait for data before composing the page.

exercise.task: Look at the home page. Find a heading, an image and a price. Identify text, an image and product data.
hints: Which stores information: the browser or the database?
exercise.solution: The database stores shop information. The browser displays it and can also keep small amounts of local information.

quiz.question: Which stores information: the browser or the database?
quiz.explanation: The database stores shop information. The browser displays it and can also keep small amounts of local information.

quiz.question: A customer opens the shop. What displays the page?
quiz.explanation: The browser turns the received response into a visible page.

quiz.question: Do the browser, server and database have exactly the same job?
quiz.explanation: They display, handle requests and store data: three complementary jobs.

summary: The database stores shop information. The browser displays it and can also keep small amounts of local information.
lessons.why: Next.js uses app/page.tsx to build the home page. HomePage prepares what visitors see; async lets it wait for data before composing the page.
lessons.whatIf: Without a page at this route, Next.js would not know what home screen to render. This file arranges the display; it does not replace the database.

teaching.why: Next.js uses app/page.tsx to build the home page. HomePage prepares what visitors see; async lets it wait for data before composing the page.
teaching.how: Next.js uses app/page.tsx to build the home page. HomePage prepares what visitors see; async lets it wait for data before composing the page.
teaching.breaks: Without a page at this route, Next.js would not know what home screen to render. This file arranges the display; it does not replace the database.
teaching.modify: Look at the home page. Find a heading, an image and a price. Identify text, an image and product data.

lessons.title: Find the parts of your site
lessons.concept: Find the parts of your site

explanation.text: A project is a set of files arranged in folders. You do not need to read everything. Find the part related to what you want to understand.
In L’ecomax, app holds pages and APIs, components holds reusable pieces, and lib holds shared functions. package.json lists tools and commands.

explanation.title: script
explanation.text: A shortcut for a terminal command.

codeExample.code:
"scripts": {
    "predev": "npm run generate:course && npm run source:refresh",
    "source:refresh": "node scripts/source-library.mjs",
    "dev": "next dev",
    "prebuild": "npm run validate:course && npm run source:refresh",
    "build": "node scripts/next-build.mjs",
    "test": "node --test tests/*.test.ts && npm run -s test:android-back",

annotations.label: These shortcuts name project commands. npm run dev runs dev; predev prepares required files just before it.

exercise.task: In this section’s file explorer, find app/page.tsx and package.json. Read their names. Explain the difference between a page and a list of tools.
hints: Where would you look for a piece used on several pages?
exercise.solution: In components. Reusing a piece avoids copying its code everywhere.

quiz.question: Where would you look for a piece used on several pages?
quiz.explanation: In components. Reusing a piece avoids copying its code everywhere.

quiz.question: You need the command to start the site. Which file should you consult?
quiz.explanation: package.json lists project commands, including dev.

quiz.question: Must you understand every file before starting a small change?
quiz.explanation: Start with the file related to your goal, then follow dependencies as needed.

summary: In components. Reusing a piece avoids copying its code everywhere.
lessons.why: These shortcuts name project commands. npm run dev runs dev; predev prepares required files just before it.
lessons.whatIf: You would need to remember full commands. This file organises tools; it does not draw a shop page.

lessons.title: Read your first line of code
lessons.concept: Read your first line of code

explanation.text:
A tag describes the role of content. In

My shop

L’ecomax .tsx files use JSX, a way to write page elements inside code. app/layout.tsx defines the shared structure.

explanation.text: HTML-like syntax used in React to describe the interface.

codeExample.code: Aller au contenu principal

lessons.title: Colour, spacing and phones

explanation.text: Content says what to display. Styling says how: colour, size and spacing. A phone layout keeps text readable and buttons easy to tap.
L’ecomax uses Tailwind. In className, p-4 adds inner spacing and rounded-xl rounds corners. sm: applies a style from a defined screen width.

explanation.title: className
explanation.text: The list of CSS classes applied to a React element.

codeExample.code:
return

{t("Ta quête · Zéro → Héros", "Your quest · Zero → Hero", "رحلتك · من الصفر إلى الاحتراف")}

annotations.label: Tailwind classes describe appearance on the element: rounded-3xl rounds corners, border adds a border, and bg-white gives a white background.

exercise.task: Compare this page in a narrow and wide window. Find something that changes position or size. On a phone, compare portrait and landscape.
hints: Does adding spacing inside a button change a price?
exercise.solution: No. Styling changes presentation. Prices belong to data and calculations.

quiz.question: Does adding spacing inside a button change a price?
quiz.explanation: No. Styling changes presentation. Prices belong to data and calculations.

quiz.question: A button feels cramped inside. Which class from the lesson helps?
quiz.explanation: p-4 adds inner spacing. rounded-xl changes the corners.

quiz.question: Should you check phone readability even if the desktop site looks good?
quiz.explanation: The width changes: text and buttons must remain usable.

summary: No. Styling changes presentation. Prices belong to data and calculations.
lessons.why: Tailwind classes describe appearance on the element: rounded-3xl rounds corners, border adds a border, and bg-white gives a white background.
lessons.whatIf: Content would remain without these visual choices. CSS changes appearance, not a product’s stored price.

lessons.title: Make a small calculation

explanation.text: A variable names a value. A function takes values and produces a result. Example: price = 10, quantity = 2, subtotal = price × quantity = 20.
L’ecomax groups checkout calculations in lib/checkout-total.ts. The final amount can also depend on shipping and discounts.
Use zero when a value is missing (null or undefined).

annotations.label: This function totals shipping, fees, taxes and discounts. minorUnits works in cents to limit rounding errors; / 100 converts back to currency units.

exercise.task: Without placing an order, calculate 3 items at €12. Add €4 shipping. Write both steps.
hints: What is the total in this example?
exercise.solution: 3 × 12 = €36, then 36 + 4 = €40. Separate steps make mistakes easier to find.

quiz.question: What is the total in this example?
quiz.explanation: 3 × 12 = €36, then 36 + 4 = €40. Separate steps make mistakes easier to find.

quiz.question: Two items at €15 and €5 shipping: what is the total?
quiz.explanation: 2 × 15 = 30, then 30 + 5 = 35. Shipping is added once in this example.

quiz.question: Can a function receive values and calculate a result?
quiz.explanation: For example, it receives price and quantity to calculate a subtotal.

summary: 3 × 12 = €36, then 36 + 4 = €40. Separate steps make mistakes easier to find.
lessons.why: This function totals shipping, fees, taxes and discounts. minorUnits works in cents to limit rounding errors; / 100 converts back to currency units.
lessons.whatIf: Duplicating this calculation across pages risks inconsistent totals. Math.max(0, …) prevents a negative discounted total.

teaching.why: This function totals shipping, fees, taxes and discounts. minorUnits works in cents to limit rounding errors; / 100 converts back to currency units.
teaching.how: This function totals shipping, fees, taxes and discounts. minorUnits works in cents to limit rounding errors; / 100 converts back to currency units.
teaching.breaks: Duplicating this calculation across pages risks inconsistent totals. Math.max(0, …) prevents a negative discounted total.

lessons.title: A reusable product card

explanation.text: A component is a reusable piece of interface. Like a mould: the shape stays the same, but you can give it another title, image and price.
CollectionProductCard.tsx describes a product card. React assembles components into a page. Information passed to a component is called props.

explanation.title: props
explanation.text: Information passed into a component, such as product here.

annotations.label: A product card is a reusable React component. It receives product as input: the same presentation can show different names, images and prices.

exercise.task: Draw two product cards: same layout, different names and prices. Circle what stays the same.
hints: Do you need a whole new card for every product?
exercise.solution: No. One component can receive different data. You can fix its appearance in one place.

quiz.question: Do you need a whole new card for every product?
quiz.explanation: No. One component can receive different data. You can fix its appearance in one place.

quiz.question: Two cards have the same layout but different prices. What varies?
quiz.explanation: Props let you supply different information to the same component.

quiz.question: Can changing a shared component change several cards?
quiz.explanation: Yes, cards using that component can all benefit from the change.

summary: No. One component can receive different data. You can fix its appearance in one place.
lessons.why: A product card is a reusable React component. It receives product as input: the same presentation can show different names, images and prices.
lessons.whatIf: Writing every card by hand makes fixes slow and inconsistent. A component lets one change improve every card.

teaching.why: A product card is a reusable React component. It receives product as input: the same presentation can show different names, images and prices.
teaching.how: A product card is a reusable React component. It receives product as input: the same presentation can show different names, images and prices.
teaching.breaks: Writing every card by hand makes fixes slow and inconsistent. A component lets one change improve every card.
teaching.modify: Draw two product cards: same layout, different names and prices. Circle what stays the same.

lessons.title: How an address opens a page
lessons.concept: How an address opens a page

explanation.text: A route connects an address to a page. Next.js uses app folders to organise routes. A part in square brackets changes with the requested page.
app/produit/[slug]/page.tsx serves product pages. In the example /produit/my-bag, my-bag is the slug: the address part identifying a product.

explanation.title: params
explanation.text: Values taken from the variable parts of a URL.

annotations.label: [slug] is the changing part of the URL. The code reads it to find the product and prepare page information.

exercise.task: Open two real products in the shop and compare their addresses. Find the shared part and the changing part.
exercise.solution: It lets one page template serve different products depending on the address.

quiz.question: What is [slug] for?
options: One page template for different products
quiz.explanation: It lets one page template serve different products depending on the address.

quiz.question: In /produit/blue-bag, which part identifies the product?
quiz.explanation: The slug is the variable part identifying the product here.

quiz.question: Does every product necessarily need a separate page.tsx file?
quiz.explanation: The [slug] route reuses the same template with different data.

summary: It lets one page template serve different products depending on the address.
lessons.why: [slug] is the changing part of the URL. The code reads it to find the product and prepare page information.
lessons.whatIf: You would need a separate page per product. A dynamic route shares the template while giving each product its own URL.

teaching.what: How an address opens a page
teaching.why: [slug] is the changing part of the URL. The code reads it to find the product and prepare page information.
teaching.how: [slug] is the changing part of the URL. The code reads it to find the product and prepare page information.

lessons.title: The page asks the server a question
lessons.concept: The page asks the server a question

explanation.text: An API is a doorway for requesting or sending data. A request is the question; a response is what the server returns. JSON is a way to organise data as text.
app/api/products/route.ts handles product-related requests. A page can request information and display a card using the response.

explanation.title: GET
explanation.text: An HTTP method used to request information.

annotations.label: GET is a read request. This route receives it, reads parameters and prepares product data. route.ts handles data; page.tsx builds a page.

exercise.task: Write this conversation: page → ‘Which products should I show?’; server → ‘Here are the products’. Add a possible response if the server is unavailable.
hints: Does a network error mean all products were deleted?
exercise.solution: No. A request can fail while the data still exists. ‘Empty’ and ‘could not load’ are different.

quiz.question: Does a network error mean all products were deleted?
options: It proves stock has run out
No, the request may have failed
quiz.explanation: No. A request can fail while the data still exists. ‘Empty’ and ‘could not load’ are different.

quiz.question: The page requests products and receives data. What is the returned message called?
quiz.explanation: The request goes to the server; the response comes back to the page.

quiz.question: Do ‘no products’ and ‘could not load products’ mean the same thing?
quiz.explanation: The first describes an empty list; the second describes a loading failure.

summary: No. A request can fail while the data still exists. ‘Empty’ and ‘could not load’ are different.
lessons.why: GET is a read request. This route receives it, reads parameters and prepares product data. route.ts handles data; page.tsx builds a page.
lessons.whatIf: The page would need another way to request server data. An API provides a contract: a defined request and an expected response.

lessons.title: Where do products live?

explanation.text: A table is like a spreadsheet: a row for each item, columns for its information. An ID helps find a row without confusing two products with the same name.
L’ecomax uses Supabase for data. lib/supabase-server.ts contains server connection code; migrations in supabase describe database changes.

explanation.title: variable d’environnement / environment variable
explanation.text: A setting supplied to a program separately from its code.

annotations.label: This code reads configuration and prepares the server connection to Supabase. process.env reads an environment variable, not product data.

exercise.task: On paper, make a table with id, name and price. Add two imaginary products with different IDs.
hints: Why keep an ID when a product has a name?
exercise.solution: A name can change or be shared. The ID identifies the intended product.

quiz.question: Why keep an ID when a product has a name?
options: To find the right product even if its name changes
quiz.explanation: A name can change or be shared. The ID identifies the intended product.

quiz.question: Two products have the same name. What should you compare to tell them apart?
quiz.explanation: An ID distinguishes one row from another even when names match.

quiz.question: Can a row represent a product and a column its price?
quiz.explanation: That is a simple way to organise a products table.

summary: A name can change or be shared. The ID identifies the intended product.
lessons.why: This code reads configuration and prepares the server connection to Supabase. process.env reads an environment variable, not product data.
lessons.whatIf: Without a valid URL and key, the server cannot use this database client. The service key must stay on the server, never in the browser.

teaching.why: This code reads configuration and prepares the server connection to Supabase. process.env reads an environment variable, not product data.
teaching.how: This code reads configuration and prepares the server connection to Supabase. process.env reads an environment variable, not product data.
teaching.breaks: Without a valid URL and key, the server cannot use this database client. The service key must stay on the server, never in the browser.

lessons.title: The door and the key

explanation.text: Signing in proves who you are. Permission decides what you may do. Hiding a button does not protect data: the server must check sensitive requests.
This section checks the owner account and a code configured on the server. Environment variables keep configuration separate from visitor-facing code.
401: identity not authenticated. 403: access forbidden.

annotations.label: The server checks identity and role before allowing owner access. This runs even when someone calls the API without using its button.

exercise.task: Draw two doors: ‘Who are you?’ and ‘Are you allowed?’. Give a customer and an owner example without copying a password.
hints: Is hiding the admin button enough to secure an API?
exercise.solution: No. The server must check identity and permission before accepting the request.

quiz.question: Is hiding the admin button enough to secure an API?
options: No, the server must check permissions
Yes, if the button is small
quiz.explanation: No. The server must check identity and permission before accepting the request.

quiz.question: A signed-in customer tries an owner-only action. What should the server do?
options: Check permissions and reject if missing
quiz.explanation: Being signed in does not automatically grant owner permissions.

quiz.question: Should a server secret be placed in code sent to visitors?
quiz.explanation: A secret must remain on the server, outside visitor-accessible code.

summary: No. The server must check identity and permission before accepting the request.
lessons.why: The server checks identity and role before allowing owner access. This runs even when someone calls the API without using its button.
lessons.whatIf: Hiding a screen is not enough: someone could call its API directly. Permission checks belong on the server.

teaching.why: The server checks identity and role before allowing owner access. This runs even when someone calls the API without using its button.
teaching.how: The server checks identity and role before allowing owner access. This runs even when someone calls the API without using its button.
teaching.breaks: Hiding a screen is not enough: someone could call its API directly. Permission checks belong on the server.
teaching.modify: Draw two doors: ‘Who are you?’ and ‘Are you allowed?’. Give a customer and an owner example without copying a password.

lessons.title: From cart to order

explanation.text: A cart is an intention to buy. An order is a record the shop tracks. The server must check products, quantities and amounts before accepting them.
app/api/orders/route.ts handles orders. Shipping calculations and product data affect the result: a price displayed in the browser is not enough as proof.

explanation.title: POST
explanation.text: An HTTP method for sending data to be processed.

annotations.label: POST sends a request that can create an order. The route must check it before saving anything: the browser is not a trusted source of prices.

exercise.task: On paper, draw product → cart → checks → order. Add ‘out of stock’ where the flow should stop. Do not create a real order.
hints: Does adding to cart mean an order is paid?
exercise.solution: No. Cart, order and payment are separate steps.

quiz.question: Does adding to cart mean an order is paid?
quiz.explanation: No. Cart, order and payment are separate steps.

quiz.question: A cart contains an out-of-stock product. When should it be checked?
quiz.explanation: The server must check availability and quantities before accepting.

quiz.question: Is a browser-supplied price enough without a server check?
quiz.explanation: The server must verify amounts against shop data.

summary: No. Cart, order and payment are separate steps.
lessons.why: POST sends a request that can create an order. The route must check it before saving anything: the browser is not a trusted source of prices.
lessons.whatIf: Without server checks, edited quantities or prices could be accepted. Study this code without creating a real order.

teaching.why: POST sends a request that can create an order. The route must check it before saving anything: the browser is not a trusted source of prices.

lessons.title: How a payment is confirmed

explanation.text: A success message in the browser is not enough proof. The server must verify payment information. A webhook is a message sent directly from a service to your server.
L’ecomax has a PayPal webhook endpoint in app/api/paypal/webhook/route.ts. An event can arrive more than once, so processing must avoid duplicates.

explanation.title: webhook
explanation.text: A server-to-server notification when an event occurs.

annotations.label: A webhook is a message PayPal sends to the server. This code verifies its signature before trusting it. A success page alone does not prove confirmed payment.

exercise.task: Write ‘same confirmation received twice’ on paper. Explain why it should not create two shipments. No real payment is needed.
hints: What could go wrong if the same event is processed twice?
exercise.solution: It could trigger an action twice, such as a notification or shipment. Previously processed events need to be recognised.

quiz.question: What could go wrong if the same event is processed twice?
quiz.explanation: It could trigger an action twice, such as a notification or shipment. Previously processed events need to be recognised.

quiz.question: The browser shows ‘payment successful’. What check is still needed?
options: Verify payment information on the server
quiz.explanation: A visible message alone is not reliable payment proof.

quiz.question: Is a webhook a message sent directly from a service to your server?
quiz.explanation: It lets the service notify the server about an event to verify and process.

summary: It could trigger an action twice, such as a notification or shipment. Previously processed events need to be recognised.
lessons.why: A webhook is a message PayPal sends to the server. This code verifies its signature before trusting it. A success page alone does not prove confirmed payment.
lessons.whatIf: A fake message could be mistaken for confirmation. This check rejects an invalid signature before further processing.

teaching.why: A webhook is a message PayPal sends to the server. This code verifies its signature before trusting it. A success page alone does not prove confirmed payment.
teaching.how: A webhook is a message PayPal sends to the server. This code verifies its signature before trusting it. A success page alone does not prove confirmed payment.
teaching.breaks: A fake message could be mistaken for confirmation. This check rejects an invalid signature before further processing.

lessons.title: Test before going live

explanation.text: Localhost is the site running on your computer. Production is the site visitors use. Local testing lets you observe a change before publishing it.
package.json defines npm run dev for development and npm run build to prepare production output. The project also contains tests and verification scripts.

explanation.title: production
explanation.text: The version real visitors use.

codeExample.code:

    "test": "node --test tests/*.test.ts && npm run -s test:android-back",
    "test:android-back": "node mobile/scripts/test-android-back.mjs",
    "test:preorder": "node --test tests/preorder.test.ts tests/preorder-api.test.ts tests/preorder-retry.test.ts tests/mobile-cart-reconciliation.test.ts && node scripts/test-preorder-sql.mjs",

annotations.label: Build prepares the site for production; dev is for local work. This project’s build script calls a program in scripts, which you can open to follow the steps.

lessons.title: See the whole shop, then keep learning
lessons.concept: See the whole shop, then keep learning

explanation.text: A shop is more than page code. It also needs photos, products, stock, deliveries, support and customers. These parts depend on one another.
The mobile folder contains the mobile app. The Academy goes deeper into code, APIs, Supabase, payments, email, design, testing, launch, sourcing, imports, SEO and growth.

explanation.title: frontend / backend
explanation.text: The customer-facing interface / server code that processes its requests.

annotations.label: The mobile folder has its own package.json: the app uses Expo and React Native. The website uses Next.js. Different interfaces can call the same shop APIs.

exercise.task: Draw a customer journey: discover → choose → order → receive → ask for help. Choose the part you want to understand next in the Academy.

exercise.solution: No. Understanding the site includes checking the whole customer journey. Continue with a detailed lesson at your own pace.
